title: What is the Well-Architected Framework (the pillars: Operational Excellence, Security, Reliability, Performance Efficiency, Cost Optimization, Sustainability), and how do you use it in a design review?
shortTitle: What is the Well-Architected Framework (the pillars), and how do you use it in a design review?

s1_definition.profdef: The Well-Architected Framework is a structured set of best-practice questions, organized into six pillars — Operational Excellence, Security, Reliability, Performance Efficiency, Cost Optimization, and Sustainability — used to review a workload's design and surface risks before they become incidents. In a design review you score the architecture against each pillar, record findings as high, medium, or low risk, and produce a prioritized remediation plan. It is not a certification; it is a repeatable lens for making deliberate trade-offs.
s1_definition.analogy: Think of it as the six-point inspection checklist that National Bank of India runs before opening a new branch. One inspector checks that the staff know how to run the branch day to day (Operational Excellence), one checks the vault and locks (Security), one checks that the branch keeps serving customers even if the power fails (Reliability), one checks that the queues move fast enough (Performance), one checks that the branch is not wasting money on an oversized building (Cost), and one checks that it is not burning more electricity than it needs (Sustainability). Every inspector writes down risks, and the branch manager fixes the serious ones before the doors open.
s1_definition.oneliner: Six pillars, one question per risk, scored before launch — it turns "it feels fine" into "here are our top three risks and the plan to close them."
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** The Well-Architected Framework is a structured set of best-practice questions, organized into six pillars — Operational Excellence, Security, Reliability, Performance Efficiency, Cost Optimization, and Sustainability — used to review a workload's design and surface risks before they become incidents. In a design review you score the architecture against each pillar, record findings as high, medium, or low risk, and produce a prioritized remediation plan. It is not a certification; it is a repeatable lens for making deliberate trade-offs.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Think of it as the six-point inspection checklist that National Bank of India runs before opening a new branch. One inspector checks that the staff know how to run the branch day to day (Operational Excellence), one checks the vault and locks (Security), one checks that the branch keeps serving customers even if the power fails (Reliability), one checks that the queues move fast enough (Performance), one checks that the branch is not wasting money on an oversized building (Cost), and one checks that it is not burning more electricity than it needs (Sustainability). Every inspector writes down risks, and the branch manager fixes the serious ones before the doors open.

**One line to remember:** Six pillars, one question per risk, scored before launch — it turns "it feels fine" into "here are our top three risks and the plan to close them."

sections.s2_technical:
Each pillar answers a different question about the workload, and a good reviewer treats them as six independent lenses on the same design. Operational Excellence asks: can you run and evolve this system smoothly? That covers whether you have infrastructure-as-code, automated deployments, runbooks, observability, and a blameless process for learning from incidents. Security asks: can you protect data and systems? That covers identity and least privilege, encryption in transit and at rest, detective controls like audit logging, and incident response. Reliability asks: does the system recover from failure and meet its availability target? That covers redundancy across availability zones, automated failover, backups, defined recovery objectives, and the discipline of actually testing recovery.

Performance Efficiency asks: are you using the right resources efficiently and can you scale? That covers choosing the right compute and storage types, caching hot data, using asynchronous processing where appropriate, and load-testing to find limits before customers do. Cost Optimization asks: are you spending only on what delivers value? That covers right-sizing instances, using auto-scaling so you pay for demand rather than peak, choosing managed services to cut operational overhead, and attributing cost back to teams with tagging so spending is visible. Sustainability, the newest pillar, asks: are you minimizing the environmental impact? That covers maximizing utilization so idle resources are not drawing power, choosing efficient regions and instance families, and deleting unused resources.

The pillars deliberately pull against each other, and recognizing those tensions is the senior-level skill. Reliability pushes you toward running redundant capacity across multiple zones, which raises cost. Performance pushes you toward over-provisioning, which also raises cost and can hurt sustainability. Security sometimes adds latency that works against raw performance. A Well-Architected review does not pretend these tensions do not exist; it makes them explicit so the business can choose. For a core payments ledger at a bank you will consciously spend more to buy reliability and security, whereas for an internal analytics job you will trade some reliability for lower cost.

How you actually run the review is a repeatable ritual. You define the workload and its business criticality, then you walk through the questions for each pillar with the architects and operators in the room. For every question you decide whether the practice is in place, and if it is not, you record a finding with a risk level — high-risk items are things that could cause data loss or an outage, medium-risk items degrade the workload, and low-risk items are minor improvements. You then produce a prioritized improvement plan, assign owners, and schedule a follow-up review, because architecture drifts over time and a review is a snapshot, not a one-time certificate. The output that matters is not a score; it is the ranked list of risks and the commitment to fix the top ones.
sections.s3_banking:
At National Bank of India the architecture guild is reviewing the new real-time payments service before it goes live. Rajesh presents the design and Priya, the reviewing architect, walks it through the six pillars. They want a tool that captures each pillar's finding, assigns a risk level, and produces the prioritized remediation list that the team will actually work through.

Problem 1 — The service deploys by someone running commands by hand, and there are no runbooks. This is exactly how an Operational Excellence gap looks — when the on-call engineer is paged at 3 a.m. there is no automated, repeatable way to recover. The tool records a high-risk Operational Excellence finding.

Problem 2 — The payments database runs in a single availability zone with no automated failover and recovery has never been tested. This is exactly how a Reliability gap looks — a single zone outage takes payments down and nobody knows how long recovery would take. The tool records a high-risk Reliability finding.

Problem 3 — Every instance is provisioned at peak size and runs twenty-four hours a day even though traffic is heavily daytime-skewed. This is exactly how a Cost and Sustainability gap looks — the bank pays for and powers capacity that sits idle most of the night. The tool records a medium-risk Cost finding.

Problem 4 — Identity uses least privilege, data is encrypted in transit and at rest, and audit logging is on. This is exactly how a strong Security posture looks — the tool records Security as compliant with no finding.

The code will model a `Pillar`, a `ReviewFinding` with a risk level, a `WellArchitectedReview` that collects findings per pillar, and a `RemediationPlanner` that sorts the findings so the high-risk items come first. We will run the four observations above and print the prioritized plan the team takes away from the review.

```
├── pom.xml
├── src/
│   ├── main/

│   │   │   │   ├── Pillar.java                      (enum)
│   │   │   │   ├── RiskLevel.java                   (enum)

│   │   │   ├── review/
│   │   │   │   └── WellArchitectedReview.java
│   │   │   └── plan/
│   │   │       └── RemediationPlanner.java
│   │   └── resources/
│   │       └── review-template.yml
│   └── test/
│       └── java/com/bank/review/
│           └── plan/
│               └── RemediationPlannerTest.java
```

Configuration file:

```yaml
# review-template.yml — the six pillars and sample questions
workload: realtime-payments
criticality: tier-1          # drives how strict the risk bar is
pillars:
  operational-excellence:
    - "Is deployment automated (IaC) and are there runbooks?"
  security:
    - "Least privilege, encryption in transit/at rest, audit logging?"
  reliability:
    - "Multi-AZ, automated failover, tested recovery, defined RTO/RPO?"
  performance-efficiency:
    - "Right-sized compute, caching, load-tested limits?"
  cost-optimization:
    - "Auto-scaling vs peak provisioning, right-sizing, cost tagging?"
  sustainability:
    - "High utilization, efficient instance families, idle cleanup?"
```
sections.s4e_build:
How you build and run it:

```bash
# Build
mvn clean package -DskipTests

# Run the Well-Architected review demo
java -cp target/classes com.bank.review.ReviewApplication
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input data: four observations about the realtime-payments service — manual deploys with no runbooks, a single-zone database with untested recovery, peak-sized round-the-clock instances, and a strong security posture.

Step 1: The application creates a review object for the workload "realtime-payments" with an empty findings list. Nothing has been judged yet.

Step 2: The first observation becomes a high-risk Operational Excellence finding. The review records it, sees it is actionable, and logs a WARNING naming the pillar, the risk, and the issue. The findings list now has one item.

Step 3: The second observation becomes a high-risk Reliability finding. The review records it and logs a WARNING. The findings list now has two items, both high-risk.

Step 4: The third observation becomes a medium-risk Cost Optimization finding. The review records it and logs a WARNING. The list now has three actionable items.

Step 5: The fourth observation is Security and it is compliant, so its risk level is none. The review records it but, because it is not actionable, it logs an INFO saying the pillar is compliant with no finding. The list has four items total, three of them actionable.

Step 6: The planner receives all four findings, filters out the non-actionable Security one, and sorts the remaining three by risk rank so the two high-risk items come before the medium one. It logs that the plan has three items and then logs each in priority order with its recommended fix.

Step 7: The final output is a ranked remediation plan. The two high-risk items — automate deployment and make the database multi-zone with tested recovery — come first, followed by the medium cost item. Security does not appear because there is nothing to fix. This is exactly the artifact the team carries out of the review.

Final output:

```
INFO: === National Bank of India — Well-Architected review: realtime-payments ===
WARNING: [OPERATIONAL_EXCELLENCE] HIGH risk: manual deployment, no runbooks
WARNING: [RELIABILITY] HIGH risk: single-AZ database, recovery never tested
WARNING: [COST_OPTIMIZATION] MEDIUM risk: peak-provisioned 24x7 despite daytime-skewed traffic
INFO: [SECURITY] compliant — no finding
INFO: Prioritized remediation plan has 3 item(s)
INFO: 1. [HIGH] OPERATIONAL_EXCELLENCE — fix: adopt IaC + automated CD pipeline, write on-call runbooks
INFO: 2. [HIGH] RELIABILITY — fix: multi-AZ with automated failover, define RTO/RPO, run DR game-days
INFO: 3. [MEDIUM] COST_OPTIMIZATION — fix: enable auto-scaling, right-size, schedule scale-down off-peak
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```text
  Design review session: realtime-payments
    │
    ▼
  WellArchitectedReview.record() × 4
    │
    ├─ Op Excellence: manual deploy ──→ HIGH   (WARNING)
    ├─ Reliability: single-AZ ─────────→ HIGH   (WARNING)
    ├─ Cost: peak 24x7 ────────────────→ MEDIUM (WARNING)
    └─ Security: least-priv+encrypt ───→ NONE   (INFO, compliant)
    │
    ▼
  RemediationPlanner.prioritize()
    │ filter actionable (drop NONE) → 3 items
    │ sort by risk rank (HIGH=1, MEDIUM=2)
    ▼
  Prioritized plan:
    1. HIGH  Op Excellence → IaC + CD + runbooks
    2. HIGH  Reliability   → multi-AZ + DR game-days
    3. MEDIUM Cost         → auto-scaling + right-size
```

sections.s5d_lld:
```
  ═══ LLD — Review + Remediation Planner ═══

  ┌─ Design Patterns Used ────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  Builder-of-report (Collector): review accumulates        │
  │     findings; planner transforms to an ordered plan.       │
  │     WHY: separates capture from prioritization.            │
  │  Strategy (via Comparator): sort order is pluggable        │
  │     (by risk now; by pillar or effort later).              │
  │     WHY: change ranking without touching the planner body. │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌─ SOLID Principles Applied ────────────────────────────────┐
  │  S: Review captures; Planner ranks; Finding is data       │
  │  O: new pillar → add enum value, logic unchanged          │
  │  L: every ReviewFinding usable wherever Finding expected  │
  │  I: Finding exposes pillar/risk/issue/remediation only    │
  │  D: Planner depends on Finding + RiskLevel abstractions   │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ── Class Diagram ───────────────────────────────────────────

  ┌──────────────────────────┐ collects ┌────────────────────────┐
  │ WellArchitectedReview    │─────────▶│ ReviewFinding          │
  │ -workload                │          │ -pillar: Pillar        │
  │ -findings: List          │          │ -risk: RiskLevel       │
  │ + record(finding)        │          │ -issue, -remediation   │
  │ + getFindings()          │          │ +isActionable()        │
  └──────────────────────────┘          └───────────┬────────────┘
                                                     │ ranked by
  ┌──────────────────────────┐ consumes             ▼
  │ RemediationPlanner       │──────────▶  RiskLevel (HIGH<MED<LOW)
  │ + prioritize(findings)   │
  └──────────────────────────┘

  ── State Diagram: a finding ────────────────────────────────

  [OBSERVED] ──record──→ [CAPTURED]
      │                      │ isActionable?
      │                      ├─ NONE → [COMPLIANT] (drop from plan)
      │                      └─ HIGH/MED/LOW → [IN_PLAN]
      ▼                                              │ assigned+fixed
  [TRACKED] ◀──────────────────── re-review ────────┘ → [RESOLVED]

  ── Call Chain (Main Scenario) ──────────────────────────────

  1. main() → new WellArchitectedReview("realtime-payments")
  2.   → review.record(OpEx HIGH)   → WARNING, list=1
  3.   → review.record(Reliab HIGH) → WARNING, list=2
  4.   → review.record(Cost MEDIUM) → WARNING, list=3
  5.   → review.record(Security NONE) → INFO compliant, list=4
  6.   → planner.prioritize(findings)
  7.     → filter actionable → 3, sort by rank
  8.     → print ranked plan (HIGH, HIGH, MEDIUM)
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
The Well-Architected Framework is a structured set of best-practice questions organized into six pillars that I use as a repeatable lens to review a workload before it goes live and periodically afterward. The six pillars are Operational Excellence, which asks whether I can run and evolve the system smoothly with automation and runbooks; Security, which asks whether I protect data and identity with least privilege, encryption, and audit logging; Reliability, which asks whether the system recovers from failure and meets its availability target with redundancy and tested recovery; Performance Efficiency, which asks whether I use the right resources and can scale; Cost Optimization, which asks whether I spend only on what delivers value; and Sustainability, which asks whether I minimize environmental impact by keeping utilization high and deleting idle resources.

The real skill is understanding that the pillars deliberately pull against each other. Reliability pushes me toward redundant capacity across zones, which raises cost. Performance tempts me to over-provision, which raises cost and hurts sustainability. Security sometimes adds latency that works against raw performance. A Well-Architected review does not pretend these tensions away — it makes them explicit so the business can make a conscious choice. For a tier-one payments ledger I will deliberately spend more to buy reliability and security, whereas for an internal analytics job I will happily trade some reliability for lower cost.

The way I actually run a review is a ritual. I define the workload and its business criticality, then I walk the questions for each pillar with the architects and operators in the room, and for every gap I record a finding with a risk level — high risk for anything that could cause data loss or an outage, medium for things that degrade the workload, and low for minor improvements. The output that matters is not a score, it is a prioritized list of risks with owners and a follow-up date, because architecture drifts and a review is a snapshot, not a certificate.

At National Bank of India I ran exactly this review on our real-time payments service and built a small tool to capture it. It flagged two high risks — we were deploying by hand with no runbooks, and our database was single-zone with recovery that had never been tested — plus a medium cost risk from running peak-sized instances around the clock, while security came back clean because we already had least privilege, encryption, and audit logging. The team walked out with a ranked plan: automate the deployment, make the database multi-zone with tested disaster-recovery game-days, and add auto-scaling to cut the idle cost — and that concrete, prioritized plan is the whole point of the framework.
